Adulterer
uh-DUL-ter-er
n.
Latin adulter, one who corrupts another's marriage, from ad- (to) + alter (other)—to turn toward another. This entry treats the person; the act has its own page.

Biblical Definition

An adulterer is the man—and the adulteress the woman—who breaks the marriage covenant sexually. This page treats the person; for the act and its ethic see Adultery. The seventh commandment is four words in English: Thou shalt not commit adultery (Exod 20:14). The Mosaic penalty names both parties without distinction of sex, which was itself remarkable in the ancient world: the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death (Lev 20:10). Christ then extends the category inward without softening it: whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart (Matt 5:28)—which makes the label reach a great many respectable men who have never touched anyone. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor 6:9), and then, four verses later, says of that whole catalogue, and such were some of you: but ye are washed—the single most important sentence for anyone reading this page about himself. The word is a description of what a man has done, not a permanent species he belongs to. Hebrews states the standing judgment plainly: Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge (Heb 13:4). Two things are said in one breath—the marriage bed is honorable and clean, and God Himself is the judge of those who defile it. No human tribunal is named, which means the sin is never actually unwitnessed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ADULTERER as a man guilty of adultery—one who has criminal intercourse with a married woman not his wife; and in Scripture, an idolater, or an apostate from the true faith.

expand to see more

ADULTERER, n. — A man guilty of adultery; a man who has sexual commerce with any married woman, except his wife.

ADULTERER, n. — In Scripture, an idolater; also, an apostate from the true faith, or one who violates his covenant engagements; a very wicked person. Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God (Jas 4:4).

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:14 — "Thou shalt not commit adultery."

Leviticus 20:10 — "And the man that committeth adultery with another man's wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour's wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death."

Matthew 5:28 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."

Hebrews 13:4 — "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge."

Modern Corruption

The category has been dissolved by consent—arrangements, openness, and the claim that pornography involves no one—while Christ's ruling makes the label reach the private man who has broken no vow visibly and broken it thoroughly in the heart.

expand to see more

The dissolving move is procedural: if all parties agree, no one has been wronged, and the word becomes an anachronism describing a bookkeeping error in an outdated contract. Scripture's marriage is not a contract between two adults but a covenant witnessed by God, which is why Hebrews 13:4 names God as the judge rather than a court or a spouse. Consent cannot license what was never the parties' to trade. The second dissolving move is technological—pornography treated as private and victimless—and Matthew 5:28 answers it directly and uncomfortably: the adultery is already accomplished in the heart, with a real person on the other side of the screen.

The church's own corruption runs the other way, and this page must say so plainly. Adulterer gets used as a permanent caste marker, a label pinned to a man for life. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 6 includes adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom—and then says such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified. Past tense. The gospel does not soften what adultery is; it moves men out of the category. A church that keeps the label after God has removed it is preaching a different message than the one Paul preached to men who had done exactly this.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew na'aph, to commit adultery, used of marital and covenant infidelity; Greek moichos, an adulterer, and moicheuō, the verb of the seventh commandment.

expand to see more

Hebrew na'aph (H5003) — to commit adultery; used both of the marital sin and of Israel's idolatry (Exod 20:14; Jer 3:8-9; Hos 4:13).

Greek moichos (G3432) — an adulterer; the noun in Paul's and the writer to the Hebrews' warnings (Luke 18:11; 1 Cor 6:9; Heb 13:4).

Greek moicheuō (G3431) — to commit adultery; the verb of the seventh commandment and of Christ's extension of it to the look (Matt 5:27-28; Rom 2:22; Jas 2:11).

Usage

"Person, not act — the ethic lives on the Adultery page; this is the man who does it."

"Leviticus 20:10 names both parties: adulterer and adulteress alike."

"Such were some of you: but ye are washed—the label is what a man did, not what he must remain."
